claims.claim: Mythgard's Exploring The Lord of the Rings is an explicitly sentence-level reading, but no transcripts or notes are published; only titles are public.
claims.source: Mythgard Institute, Exploring the Lord of the Rings project page

claims.claim: The Council of Elrond succeeds by representing many tongues, with Gandalf performing the voice of each speaker he reports, from Saruman to the Gaffer and Butterbur.
claims.source: John Halbrooks, 'Could The Council of Elrond Have Been an Email?'

claims.claim: Art is the achievement of expression that gives a Secondary World the inner consistency of reality; consistency, not novelty, is what earns belief.

claims.feature: Secondary Belief vs suspension of disbelief
claims.claim: Inside a successful Secondary World what is related is 'true' by that world's own laws, and the instant a reader's disbelief arises the art has failed — suspension of disbelief is only a substitute for genuine Secondary Belief.
claims.quote: The moment disbelief arises, the spell is broken

claims.claim: Fantasy's native advantage is arresting strangeness, which must be married to consistency or it decays into the merely fanciful and decorative.
The more the images depart from the Primary World the harder inner consistency is to produce, so fantastic material demands more labour than sober material, not less.
claims.quote: easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material

claims.claim: Anyone can say 'the green sun'; building a world in which it commands Secondary Belief requires labour, thought and a special elvish craft — narrative art in its most potent mode.
The adjective is the root spell of Faërie: to take green from grass or red from blood is already an enchanter's power, so fantasy is built at the level of the word.
claims.quote: a part of speech in a mythical grammar

claims.claim: Fantasy's function of Recovery is regaining a clear view, freeing familiar things from the triteness of appropriation — the prose must make the known strange again.
claims.quote: the drab blur of triteness or familiarity

claims.feature: fantasy belongs to words, not pictures or drama
claims.claim: Fantasy is best left to words because painting makes the fantastic technically too easy and Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy — the verbal medium is the proper one.
claims.quote: Fantasy is a thing best left to words

claims.claim: Faërie is indescribable though not imperceptible; the writer gives glimpses rather than definitions, and analysis will not discover the secret of the whole.
claims.quote: cannot be caught in a net of words

claims.claim: The association of fairy-stories with children is a historical accident, so the register must not be pitched down to a nursery audience.
claims.quote: an accident of our domestic history

claims.claim: The fairy-story's true form is the sudden joyous turn that denies universal defeat without denying sorrow, so the prose must carry grief and joy in one register.
A fairy-story must be presented as true and cannot tolerate any frame or machinery suggesting the whole is a figment or illusion.
The instinct of linguistic invention is the fitting of notion to oral symbol and pleasure in contemplating the relation — words must sound like what they mean.
claims.source: Tolkien, 'A Secret Vice' (full text, gwern PDF)
claims.quote: the fitting of notion to oral symbol

verdicts.trueWording: “we read through a portion of the text, sentence by sentence”
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: no transcripts or notes are published; only titles are public
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200, 65,817 B) and tag-stripped: the quote is verbatim in the 'Deep Reading and Commentary' block. The page never uses the word 'transcript' (grep -ic transcript = 0) and says nothing about notes or about only titles being public; on the contrary it advertises 'All episodes are recorded and added to the Signum University YouTube channel' plus a podcast feed, Twitch livestreams, Discord and a discussion forum, so the second limb is unsupported and in tension with the page.

verdicts.trueWording: “extends it to the representation, literally, of ‘many tongues,’ of polyglossia”
verdicts.note: Raw HTML fetched (curl, browser UA, HTTP 200, 205,319 B). Quote 'of polyglossia' appears verbatim ('of polyglossia' — contiguous as rendered). Every limb supported: '“The Council of Elrond” demonstrates this technical mastery in microcosm and extends it to the representation, literally, of “many tongues,” of polyglossia'; 'The extraordinary success of this chapter'; and Gandalf 'puts on a performance worthy of Meryl Streep, playing all of the parts himself, taking on the tongues of Saruman, Isildur, Gollum, Sauron (in the Ring's inscription), Radagast the Brown, Gwaihir the Windlord (an eagle), Gaffer Gamgee, and Butterbur the Innkeeper.'

verdicts.trueWording: “The achievement of the expression, which gives … ‘the inner consistency of reality,’ … Art”
verdicts.note: PDF downloaded (HTTP 200, 560,795 B, 41 pp) and text-extracted with pdfminer; quote occurs 5x. Limb 1 verbatim: 'The achievement of the expression, which gives (or seems to give) “the inner consistency of reality,” is indeed another thing, or aspect, needing another name: Art, the operative link between Imagination and the final result, Sub-creation.' Limb 2 (consistency, not novelty, earns belief) supported on the same page: belief follows because 'it accords with the laws of that world', while mere novelty is 'not enough' — 'Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun … But that is not enough'. The words 'a Secondary World' are the claim's gloss for Tolkien's 'ideal creations'/Sub-creation, which the essay uses interchangeably.

verdicts.trueWording: “Inside it, what he relates is ‘true’: it accords with the laws of that world”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim: 'The moment disbelief arises, the spell is broken; the magic, or rather art, has failed.' Every limb verbatim on the page: 'He makes a Secondary World which your mind can enter. Inside it, what he relates is “true”: it accords with the laws of that world'; 'this suspension of disbelief is a substitute for the genuine thing, a subterfuge'; 'A real enthusiast for cricket is in the enchanted state: Secondary Belief.'

verdicts.trueWording: “Fantasy, of course, starts out with an advantage: arresting strangeness”
verdicts.note: Same PDF; 'arresting strangeness' occurs once, in 'Fantasy, of course, starts out with an advantage: arresting strangeness.' Second limb supported in the immediately following paragraph: 'Fantasy has also an essential drawback: it is difficult to achieve … “the inner consistency of reality” is more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images … Fantasy thus, too often, remains undeveloped; it is and has been used frivolously, or only half-seriously, or merely for decoration: it remains merely “fanciful.”'

verdicts.trueWording: “more difficult to produce, the more unlike are the images … to the Primary World”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim including its curly quotes: 'It is easier to produce this kind of “reality” with more “sober” material.' Preceding sentence supplies the first limb verbatim; the 'more labour' limb is supported by 'Fantasy has also an essential drawback: it is difficult to achieve' and, on the next page, 'will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill'.

verdicts.trueWording: “require labour and thought … a special skill, a kind of elvish craft”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Whole claim verbatim in one passage: 'Anyone inheriting the fantastic device of human language can say the green sun … To make a Secondary World inside which the green sun will be credible, commanding Secondary Belief, will probably require labour and thought, and will certainly demand a special skill, a kind of elvish craft … then we have a rare achievement of Art: indeed narrative art, storymaking in its primary and most potent mode.'

verdicts.trueWording: “the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim: 'such incantations might indeed be said to be only another view of adjectives, a part of speech in a mythical grammar.' Limbs supported verbatim in the same paragraph: 'how stimulating … was the invention of the adjective: no spell or incantation in Faerie is more potent'; 'When we can take green from grass, blue from heaven, and red from blood, we have already an enchanter's power'; and 'in such “fantasy,” as it is called, new form is made; Faerie begins' — i.e. built at the level of the word.

verdicts.trueWording: “Recovery … is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view”; triteness is “the penalty of ‘appropriation’”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim: 'freed from the drab blur of triteness or familiarity—from possessiveness.' Limbs verbatim: 'Recovery (which includes return and renewal of health) is a re-gaining—regaining of a clear view'; 'This triteness is really the penalty of “appropriation”.' The prose-application limb ('make the known strange again') is the page's own idea in other words: 'We should look at green again, and be startled anew' and Chesterton's Mooreeffoc, 'the queerness of things that have become trite, when they are seen suddenly from a new angle.'

verdicts.trueWording: “In human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim inside 'In human art Fantasy is a thing best left to words, to true literature.' Both reasons verbatim on the same page: 'In painting, for instance, the visible presentation of the fantastic image is technically too easy; the hand tends to outrun the mind' and 'But Drama is naturally hostile to Fantasy.'

verdicts.trueWording: “indescribable, though not imperceptible”; “analysis will not necessarily discover the secret”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim: 'Faërie cannot be caught in a net of words; for it is one of its qualities to be indescribable, though not imperceptible.' Glimpses-not-definitions limb verbatim: 'I will not attempt to define that, nor to describe it directly. It cannot be done … will give some glimpses of my own imperfect vision of it.' One nuance: the page hedges — 'analysis will not NECESSARILY discover the secret of the whole' — where the claim drops 'necessarily'; the limb is supported but stated more categorically than Tolkien states it.

verdicts.trueWording: “the association of children and fairy-stories is an accident of our domestic history”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim. The register limb is supported in substance on the same page: adapting fairy-stories for children is 'a dangerous process'; 'Fairystories banished in this way, cut off from a full adult art, would in the end be ruined'; and 'If fairy-story as a kind is worth reading at all it is worthy to be written for and read by adults.'

verdicts.trueWording: “The eucatastrophic tale is the true form of fairy-tale”; Joy “poignant as grief”
verdicts.note: Same PDF. Quote verbatim: 'giving a fleeting glimpse of Joy, Joy beyond the walls of the world, poignant as grief.' Limbs verbatim: 'The eucatastrophic tale is the true form of fairy-tale, and its highest function'; 'the sudden joyous “turn”'; 'It does not deny the existence of dyscatastrophe, of sorrow and failure … it denies … universal final defeat.' The one-register prose gloss is carried by 'poignant as grief' itself.

verdicts.trueWording: “it cannot tolerate any frame or machinery suggesting … a figment or illusion”
verdicts.note: Raw wikitext fetched via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Special:Export/On_Fairy-Stories (HTTP 200, 23,951 B), not a summarizer. The article quotes Tolkien in full: 'It is at any rate essential to a genuine fairy-story … that it should be presented as “true”. … But since the fairy-story deals with “marvels”, it cannot tolerate any frame or machinery suggesting that the whole framework in which they occur is a figment or illusion.' Both limbs verbatim; the claim's quote “presented as ‘true’” matches.

verdicts.trueWording: “the fitting of notion to oral symbol, and pleasure in contemplating the new relation”
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: words must sound like what they mean
verdicts.note: PDF downloaded from gwern (HTTP 200, 957,151 B, 26 pp — the 'A Secret Vice' text as printed in The Monsters and the Critics) and text-extracted with pdfminer. Quote verbatim: 'The instinct for “linguistic invention” - the fitting of notion to oral symbol, and pleasure in contemplating the new relation established, is rational, and not perverted.' The essay locates the pleasure in the contemplated RELATION between sound and notion — 'it is the contemplation of the relation between sound and notion which is a main source of pleasure', 'a private sense of fitness', 'word-form in relation to meaning (so-called phonetic fitness)' — an invented, personal fitness, not mimicry. Nowhere does the page prescribe that words must sound like what they mean; that limb is the claim's own gloss.
